title: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
summary: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is the detective phase of data science where you investigate a dataset to understand its structure, spot problems, and discover patterns before building models. A systematic EDA moves through three levels: univariate a
content:
# Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) ##### The 97% accurate model that was reading the answer A team in Chandigarh built a model to predict which loan applications would be approved. Cross-validated accuracy: 97.3%. They were delighted for about a day. Then a reviewer asked a simple EDA question nobody had asked: *what does the column `officer_remark_code` actually contain?* It was populated by the loan officer **after** the decision. Code `A1` appeared on 99.4% of approved applications. The model had learned to read the answer. It would have been useless in production, where that field is empty at prediction time. Two hours of exploratory analysis at the start would have caught it. A correlation check would have shown one feature at r = 0.96 with the target — a number so high it should always trigger suspicion rather than celebration. EDA is the phase where you get to know your data before you commit to anything. John Tukey, who named it in 1977, framed it as detective work: you are looking for clues, not confirming a theory. It is unglamorous, it takes real time, and skipping it is how good teams ship bad models. ##### The EDA mindset Three principles distinguish real exploration from clicking through `describe()`. **Be sceptical, not confirmatory.** The goal is to find out what is wrong and what is surprising, not to validate what you already believe. A finding that supports your hypothesis deserves *more* scrutiny than one that contradicts it. **Question every convenient result.** A feature with r = 0.96 to the target is almost never a brilliant discovery; it is almost always leakage, a duplicate column, or a definitional artefact. High accuracy before you have done any work is a red flag. **Follow the domain, not just the statistics.** A value of `-1` in an age column is not a small number, it is a sentinel for "unknown". Only someone who asks the data owner will find that out. The systematic sequence: ```mermaid flowchart TD A[0. Understand the context
What decision? What does each column mean?] --> B[1. Structure
shape, dtypes, memory, sample rows] B --> C[2. Quality
missing, duplicates, impossible values] C --> D[3. Univariate
one variable at a time] D --> E[4. Bivariate
pairs, especially vs the target] E --> F[5. Multivariate
interactions, correlation structure] F --> G[6. Anomalies
outliers, leakage, suspicious patterns] G --> H[7. Synthesise
findings, hypotheses, next steps] H --> C ``` Note the loop back from synthesis to quality. Every finding raises a new question about the data, and good EDA cycles rather than running once. ##### Step 0–2: context, structure, quality Before any code, get answers to: what decision does this data support, what does each column actually mean, who produces it and when, and what would a domain expert consider impossible? A data dictionary — even a rough one you write yourself — is worth an hour. ```python import pandas as pd, numpy as np df = pd.read_csv("applications.csv") print(df.shape) print(df.dtypes.value_counts()) print(df.head(3).T) # transposed: readable with many columns print(df.sample(5, random_state=42).T) # sample, not just head — head can be sorted print(df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e6, "MB") quality = pd.DataFrame({ "dtype": df.dtypes, "missing_pct": (df.isna().mean() * 100).round(1), "unique": df.nunique(), "unique_pct": (df.nunique() / len(df) * 100).round(1), "top_value": [df[c].value_counts().index[0] if df[c].notna().any() else None for c in df.columns], "top_freq_pct": [(df[c].value_counts(normalize=True).iloc[0] * 100).round(1) if df[c].notna().any() else None for c in df.columns], }) print(quality.sort_values("missing_pct", ascending=False)) print("exact duplicate rows:", df.duplicated().sum()) ``` `df.sample()` rather than only `df.head()` matters — files are often sorted, so the first five rows are unrepresentative. Two columns in that quality table earn their place. **`unique_pct` near 100%** flags an identifier (useless as a feature) or free text. **`top_freq_pct` near 100%** flags a constant column, which carries no information and should be dropped. ##### Step 3: univariate analysis One variable at a time. What is its shape, its range, its typical value, and does anything look wrong? ```python import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid") num_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns cat_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=["object", "category"]).columns # Numeric: distribution grid n = len(num_cols) fig, axes = plt.subplots((n + 2) // 3, 3, figsize=(15, 3.2 * ((n + 2) // 3))) for ax, col in zip(axes.flat, num_cols): sns.histplot(df[col].dropna(), bins=30, kde=True, ax=ax) ax.axvline(df[col].median(), color="#38a169", lw=1.5) ax.axvline(df[col].mean(), color="#e53e3e", ls="--", lw=1.5) ax.set_title(f"{col} (skew {df[col].skew():.2f})", fontsize=10) for ax in axes.flat[n:]: ax.set_visible(False) fig.tight_layout() # Categorical: frequency for col in cat_cols: vc = df[col].value_counts(dropna=False) print(f"\n{col} ({df[col].nunique()} distinct)") print(vc.head(10)) if df[col].nunique() > 50: print(" ^ high cardinality — check for inconsistent spellings") ``` What to look for in each numeric distribution: is it symmetric, skewed, or bimodal? Are there spikes at suspicious values (a pile-up at exactly 0, or at 999, or at the maximum — all classic sentinel-value or capping artefacts)? Is the range plausible? For categoricals: how many distinct values, is one category dominant, and are there near-duplicate spellings? A `city` column with 340 distinct values in a dataset covering 12 cities is the Bengaluru problem from cleaning day, and univariate EDA is where you catch it. ##### Step 4: bivariate analysis Relationships between pairs — and above all, between each feature and the target. ```python TARGET = "approved" # Numeric vs categorical target for col in num_cols[:6]: fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6)) sns.boxplot(data=df, x=TARGET, y=col, ax=axes[0]) sns.kdeplot(data=df, x=col, hue=TARGET, common_norm=False, fill=True, alpha=0.35, ax=axes[1]) axes[0].set_title(f"{col} by {TARGET}") fig.tight_layout() grp = df.groupby(TARGET)[col].agg(["mean", "median", "std", "count"]) print(f"\n{col}\n{grp.round(2)}") # Categorical vs categorical target — rate per category for col in cat_cols[:6]: rates = (df.groupby(col)[TARGET].agg(["mean", "count"]) .rename(columns={"mean": "approval_rate"}) .query("count >= 30") # ignore tiny groups .sort_values("approval_rate", ascending=False)) print(f"\n{col}\n{rates.round(3)}") ``` That `count >= 30` filter is important. A category with 3 rows and a 100% approval rate is noise, and presenting it as a finding is how EDA misleads. Numeric-versus-numeric relationships: ```python fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5)) sns.regplot(data=df, x="income_inr", y="loan_amount_inr", lowess=True, scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.3, "s": 15}, line_kws={"color": "#e53e3e"}, ax=ax) ax.set_title("Is this relationship actually linear?", loc="left") ``` `lowess=True` fits a local smoother instead of a straight line, which reveals curvature that a Pearson correlation would hide. ##### Step 5: multivariate analysis ```python num = df[num_cols] corr = num.corr() mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr, dtype=bool)) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 8)) sns.heatmap(corr, mask=mask, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="coolwarm", center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1, square=True, linewidths=0.5, ax=ax) ax.set_title("Correlation matrix", loc="left") # Highly correlated pairs — both a leakage check and a multicollinearity check pairs = (corr.where(~mask).stack().reset_index() .rename(columns={"level_0": "a", "level_1": "b", 0: "r"})) print(pairs.reindex(pairs.r.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index).head(10)) # Interactions — does the effect of one variable depend on another? sns.lmplot(data=df, x="income_inr", y="loan_amount_inr", hue="employment_type", col="region", height=4, scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.35, "s": 15}) ``` The pairwise correlation list serves two purposes at once. Any feature correlating above ~0.9 with the **target** is a leakage suspect — that is the check that would have saved the Chandigarh team. Any two *features* correlating above ~0.9 with each other are redundant, which destabilises linear model coefficients. Interaction plots are where genuine insight often lives. "Income predicts loan size" is obvious. "Income predicts loan size strongly for salaried applicants and barely at all for self-employed ones" is a finding that changes how you model. ##### Step 6: outliers and anomalies ```python def outlier_summary(df, cols): rows = [] for c in cols: s = df[c].dropna() q1, q3 = s.quantile([0.25, 0.75]); iqr = q3 - q1 iqr_out = ((s < q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | (s > q3 + 1.5 * iqr)).sum() z_out = (np.abs((s - s.mean()) / s.std()) > 3).sum() rows.append({"column": c, "iqr_outliers": iqr_out, "iqr_pct": round(iqr_out / len(s) * 100, 1), "z_outliers": z_out, "min": s.min(), "max": s.max()}) return pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("iqr_pct", ascending=False) print(outlier_summary(df, num_cols)) ``` Beyond statistical outliers, look for the patterns that indicate broken data: ```python # Suspicious repeated values — sentinels hiding as data for c in num_cols: top = df[c].value_counts(normalize=True).head(1) if top.iloc[0] > 0.10: print(f"{c}: value {top.index[0]} appears in {top.iloc[0]:.1%} of rows") # Impossible combinations — domain rules print(df[(df["age"] < 18) & (df["employment_years"] > 5)].shape) print(df[df["loan_amount_inr"] > df["income_inr"] * 20].shape) # Structure in missingness print(df.isna().sum(axis=1).value_counts().head()) # rows missing k fields print(df.groupby(df["income_inr"].isna())[TARGET].mean()) # is missingness predictive? ``` That last line is a genuinely useful trick: if the *fact* that income is missing predicts the target, missingness is informative and should become a feature rather than being imputed away. ##### Automated EDA tools ```python from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport profile = ProfileReport(df, title="Loan Applications EDA", explorative=True, minimal=False) profile.to_file("eda_report.html") ``` One line produces distributions for every column, correlation matrices in four methods, missing-value patterns, duplicate detection, high-cardinality and constant-column warnings, and interaction plots. On a 40-column dataset it saves genuine hours. `sweetviz` and `dtale` are alternatives worth knowing. What these tools do well: exhaustive coverage, catching things you would not have thought to check, and speed on wide datasets. What they cannot do: know that `officer_remark_code` is populated after the decision. Know that `-1` means unknown in this system. Know which of two correlated features is causally upstream. Know what question you are trying to answer, and therefore which of 400 generated charts matters. **Use automated profiling as a first pass, then do targeted manual EDA on what it flags.** The tool finds the anomalies; you supply the judgement about which ones matter. Note also that these tools slow down badly above a few hundred thousand rows — sample first. ##### Step 7: synthesising findings EDA that produces no written output was not EDA. Close every exploration with a structured summary: ```markdown ## EDA Findings — Loan Applications ### Data quality 1. `officer_remark_code` correlates 0.96 with the target and is populated post-decision. LEAKAGE — must be excluded. (Confirmed with the ops team.) 2. `income_inr` has 14% missing, and missingness itself predicts approval (38% vs 61%). MNAR — add a missingness flag rather than imputing away. 3. 2,847 duplicate `application_id` values from a re-import on 2026-03-14. 4. `age` contains 61 values of -1 used as "unknown". ### Distributions 5. Loan amount is heavily right-skewed (skew 2.8); log transform reduces to 0.2. 6. Approval rate is 31% — moderately imbalanced, use PR-AUC not accuracy. ### Relationships 7. Income and loan amount correlate at 0.71, but the relationship is non-linear above ₹20 lakh (lowess shows a plateau). 8. `employment_type` interacts with income: the income effect is strong for salaried applicants and near-flat for self-employed. ### Hypotheses to test H1: A debt-to-income ratio feature will outperform income and loan amount separately. H2: Applications submitted in the last three days of a month are approved at a higher rate (target-chasing behaviour) — needs a date-based check. ### Next steps - Exclude the leakage column; rebuild the baseline. - Engineer DTI ratio and month-end flag. - Use temporal validation; the approval rate shifts across 2025-2026. ``` That document is the actual deliverable. It is what a reviewer reads, what stops the next person repeating your work, and — as the leakage line demonstrates — what prevents a very expensive mistake. ##### Common mistakes - Skipping EDA because the model "already works". - Celebrating a suspiciously strong feature instead of investigating it. - Only running `head()` on a sorted file, seeing an unrepresentative sample. - Reporting rates for categories with three observations. - Treating a Pearson correlation as evidence of a linear relationship without plotting it. - Ignoring missingness patterns instead of testing whether they are informative. - Running an automated profiler and calling it done. - Not asking the data owner what a column actually means. - Exploring without writing anything down. - Random train/test splitting before noticing the data has a time dimension. ##### Hands-on Take an unfamiliar dataset and work through all seven steps. Force yourself through step 0 first: write a one-line definition of every column, and mark the ones you had to guess — those are the ones to ask about. Then run the structure and quality checks, produce the univariate grid, examine every feature against the target, build the correlation matrix and inspect the top ten absolute correlations, and run the outlier and anomaly checks. Write down at least five insights, and for each, state whether it is a data-quality problem, a modelling implication, or a business finding. For the mini-project, produce a full EDA report notebook on a real dataset — a Kaggle competition dataset or something from data.gov.in works well. Structure it in the seven steps with Markdown headings, keep every figure paired with an interpretation, and end with the structured findings document above: quality issues, distributions, relationships, hypotheses, next steps. The notebook should be readable top to bottom by someone who has never seen the data. For the assignment, run `ydata-profiling` on the same dataset and compare its report to your manual EDA. Write specifically about what the tool caught that you missed, and — more importantly — what your judgement caught that no automated tool could have: leakage, sentinel values, domain-impossible combinations, and which of its many findings actually matter for the question you are answering. ##### Key takeaways - EDA is detective work — you are hunting for what is wrong and surprising, not confirming what you expect. - A feature correlating above 0.9 with the target is a leakage suspect, not a discovery. - Move systematically: structure, quality, univariate, bivariate, multivariate, anomalies, synthesis. - Missingness patterns are often informative; test whether missingness itself predicts the target. - Automated profilers give coverage, not judgement — use them first, then explore what they flag, and always write your findings down.
practical_task_reference: Perform a complete EDA on an unfamiliar dataset: examine each variable's distribution, check for missing values and outliers, explore correlations, and write down at least five insights you discover.
mini_project_reference: Create a full EDA report notebook on a real dataset (e.g., a Kaggle dataset) that includes data overview, univariate/bivariate/multivariate analysis, outlier detection, and a summary of key findings and hypotheses.
assignment_reference: Run ydata-profiling on a dataset and compare its automated report to your own manual EDA, noting what the tool missed that your judgment caught.
